abstracts.abstract: Understanding the dynamic reorganization of biological networks during cellular state transitions remains a fundamental challenge in systems biology. Current computational approaches predominantly employ static graph representations that inadequately capture the temporal evolution of molecular interactions. We introduce Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (T-ERGM), a novel theoretical framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes biological network analysis by modeling time-evolving topological structures through stochastic processes. Our framework extends traditional exponential random graph models by incorporating temporal dependency structures and state-dependent edge formation probabilities, enabling rigorous statistical inference of network dynamics. We develop a maximum pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure combined with Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation for computational tractability. Validation on synthetic networks with known ground truth demonstrates superior performance (AUC = 0.91) compared to dynamic network analysis baselines. Application to time-course transcriptomic data from human embryonic stem cell differentiation reveals evolutionarily conserved rewiring patterns in gene regulatory networks that precede phenotypic transitions. The framework successfully identifies critical transition points and predicts downstream network reconfiguration with 78% accuracy. This work establishes a new theoretical paradigm for analyzing temporal biological networks, providing principled statistical methodology for understanding how cellular systems reconfigure their interaction architectures during dynamic biological processes. The T-ERGM framework is freely available as an R package enabling widespread adoption.

Accurate multiple sequence alignment (MSA) constitutes a cornerstone of computational biology, yet current state-of-the-art algorithms face significant scalability challenges when processing genome-scale sequence collections containing thousands of sequences. Progressive alignment heuristics, while computationally efficient, often sacrifice accuracy due to their greedy nature and uniform sequence weighting strategies. We present Adaptive Weighted Progressive Alignment (AWPA), a substantially improved theoretical framework that addresses these limitations through three key innovations. First, we introduce a machine learning-based approach for estimating position-specific gap penalties that adapt dynamically based on local sequence context and evolutionary conservation. Second, we develop a novel iterative refinement procedure that incorporates probabilistic consistency transformations guided by hidden Markov model posterior probabilities. Third, we propose an adaptive sequence weighting scheme that accounts for both sequence similarity and phylogenetic relatedness to mitigate sampling bias. Comprehensive benchmarking on BAliBASE 4, OXBench-X, and HOMD reference datasets demonstrates significant improvements. On datasets comprising 500-2000 sequences with less than 40% identity, AWPA achieves 12-18% higher SP-score and 15-22% higher TC-score compared to MAFFT-L-INS-i and Clustal Omega. Computational complexity remains O(N²L) for N sequences of length L, with practical runtime improvements of 2-4x through optimized implementation. This work provides a substantially improved methodology for large-scale multiple sequence alignment, enabling accurate analysis of whole-genome sequence families previously intractable to high-quality alignment.

The exponential growth of single-cell RNA sequencing data presents unprecedented computational infrastructure challenges, as existing analysis tools were not designed for datasets comprising millions of cells with high-dimensional expression profiles. We introduce scVerse, a novel distributed computing platform that fundamentally reconceptualizes single-cell genomics analysis through a streaming-first architecture and unified application programming interface. Unlike existing frameworks that load entire datasets into memory, scVerse processes single-cell data through a pipelined streaming approach, enabling analysis of datasets exceeding available RAM by an order of magnitude. The platform implements a graph-based execution engine with lazy evaluation semantics, automatically optimizing computational workflows through intelligent operator fusion and memory-aware task scheduling. We design novel data structures for sparse single-cell expression representation that achieve 4x memory reduction compared to conventional formats while enabling efficient random access for downstream analysis. The system provides native support for trajectory inference, cellular state classification, and cross-modality integration through a modular plugin architecture. Validation on published datasets comprising up to 4 million cells demonstrates linear scalability across distributed computing clusters and processing times reduced from days to minutes for standard workflows. scVerse enables systematic analysis of cellular heterogeneity across large cohort studies, including integration of multiple batches and modalities. The platform represents a paradigm shift in single-cell bioinformatics infrastructure, transforming how researchers interact with and derive insights from massive single-cell atlases.

Accurate clinical variant interpretation requires comprehensive integration of population frequency data, computational pathogenicity predictions, and curated clinical evidence from heterogeneous resources. Existing annotation pipelines suffer from fragmented data sources, redundant computational overhead, and inconsistent formatting, necessitating manual synthesis that impedes genomic medicine implementation. We present ClinVarX 2.0, a substantially enhanced variant annotation system that achieves order-of-magnitude improvements in annotation speed and completeness through innovative system architecture. The platform introduces a pre-computed variant knowledge graph with hierarchical indexing structures that enable sub-second queries across population databases including gnomAD, TOPMed, and regional population studies. We implement an ensemble pathogenicity scoring module that dynamically weights predictions from 14 computational tools based on variant context and protein domain annotations, achieving superior classification performance (F1 = 0.89) compared to individual predictors. The system architecture employs a microservices design with intelligent caching at multiple levels, reducing redundant computation across annotation batches by 73%. ClinVarX 2.0 processes whole-exome sequences in approximately 8 minutes compared to 6-12 hours with conventional pipelines, while providing 40% more comprehensive annotations including regulatory region effects and structural variant context. The platform integrates seamlessly with existing clinical workflows through standard file formats and application programming interfaces. Performance benchmarking demonstrates that ClinVarX 2.0 enables clinical variant interpretation at scale previously achievable only through time-intensive manual curation, substantially accelerating genomic medicine deployment.
